text.p: CS First Boston on Monday rated shares in Hungarian pharmaceuticals firm Egis as 'buy' saying it appears to trade at an unwarranted discount relative to Richter and its industry peer group.
"Egis is our top buy recommendation on the Hungarian market," CSFB's Budapest-based analyst Spencer Jakab said in a company report.
"We favour switching from Richter into Egis," Jakab said.

Jakab added that Egis was undervalued on several measures, including an analysis of enterprise value to invested capital as a function on return on invested capital, compared to many in the international industry peer group.
The analyst also said he disagreed with those who said that the pace of Egis's profit growth faltered.
"The widespread view that Egis has entered a profitability slump is, in our view, misleading," Jakab said. "In fact, Egis has boosted real profitability, despite slower earnings/share (EPS) growth."

Despite the fact that the two companies are present in many of the same export markets, they are not competitors and the degree of overlap between them is zero in terms of active ingredients and is minimal in terms of therapeutic areas, he said.

The two companies also differ in terms of their exposure to the Hungarian market and the current growth outlook of their topselling branded generics, both of which favour Richter in the short-run, Jakab said.
Egis generates somewhat more than half of its sales on the domestic market, while Richter makes one-third of its sales in Hungary.

"The long-run earnings outlook of the two companies, however, is similar...thus the 33.8 percent EV/EBIDTA (enterprise value/earnings before interest, dividend, tax and attributable) discount at which Egis trades to Richter appears, in our view, to be unjustified," Jakab said.
Egis registered a nominal EPS growth of 129 percent in 1993, 126 percent in 1994, 75 percent in 1995 and 14.4 percent in 1996, the analyst said.

"Underlying profitability has actually improved as return on equity has more than doubled since 1993 and and ROIC (return on invested capital), has risen from 12.7 percent in 1993 to 17.5 percent in 1996," Jakab said.
On the Budapest Stock Exchange on Monday, Egis closed at 9,755 forints, up 305, and Richter at 11,100 forints, up 240.
